description: Iodine is a chemical element with symbol I and atomic number 53. It is the heaviest of the stable halogens and exists at standard conditions as a semi-lustrous, non-metallic solid that melts to form a deep violet liquid at 114 °C and boils to a violet gas at 184 °C. The element was discovered by French chemist Bernard Courtois in 1811 and named by Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac after the Ancient Greek word for 'violet'.
uses: As the heaviest essential mineral nutrient, iodine is required for the synthesis of thyroid hormones and is on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines. Due to its high atomic number and ease of attachment to organic compounds, iodine is used as a non-toxic radiocontrast material, and radioactive isotopes of iodine can be used to treat thyroid cancer. It is also used as a catalyst in the industrial production of acetic acid and some polymers.
characteristics: Iodine is the weakest oxidizing agent among the stable halogens with an electronegativity of 2.66 on the Pauling scale and has the lowest first ionization energy and lowest reactivity among stable halogens. It is slightly soluble in water and forms diatomic molecules with the chemical formula I₂, appearing violet as a solid and gas but brown in polar solutions due to charge-transfer complexes. Iodine has the largest atomic radius among stable halogens and is a two-dimensional semiconductor with the weakest interhalogen bond among stable halogens.
